FOR FIRST PUBLICATION TUESDAY'S EVENINGS 2.7.46.

BRITAIN'S ROLLERS MAKE THE ROADS OF THE WORLD.
July 1946
Britain has long been famous in the production of road
rollers and other types of road construction machinery,
and the "Invicta" horse of the products of Messrs Aveling-
Barford of Grantham is to be seen even in the most out
of the way spots of the globe. The latest order received
by this firm is for a million pounds worth of road rollers
destined for use in all parts of India. Besides this huge
order, they have others in hand worth threefold for the
supply of machinery to all parts - from Iceland in the
north to New Zealand in the south, and only lack of labour
and further supplies of raw materials prevents the accept-
ance of additional contracts. This work has not been gained
by sitting at home - their representatives have travelled
the world and the result of their missions is seen today in
the increased activity in the Grantham factory, as illustrated
by the accompanying pictures : -

Front rollers of "GD" ten-ton roller being packed
ready for export.

23. 1. 56.

MAKING NEW RIGGING FOR NELSON'S FLAGSHIP "VICTORY"

A team of men and women have started work at Chatham
to make a complete new rigging for Nelson's Flagship,
"VICTORY". They are working in the same timber-built
rope "walks" used by the men who refitted Victory for
Trafalgar after she had been five years in the Medway
as a prison hospital ship. The work is being carried
out at Chatham's Ropery - the Admiralty's only rope-
making establishment. Methods of making the rope are
almost the same as in the days of Nelson, except that
women are employed in some of the operations, now done
by machines.

which is 1,128 feet in length. It is

---
MAKING BASKETS FOR THE FRUIT SEASON.  E. M./MAE.

There is a big demand for fruit baskets from the orchard
districts at this time and Severnside basket makers are
working long hours to try and meet it.  Foreign competition
has, of recent years, had a discouraging effect on the basket-
making trade which, in this district, has been carried on as
a family art throughout the years.  The withies from which
the baskets are made grow on the banks of the river and after
two or three years drying, are boiled in special outdoor
boilers to make them supple.  One of the "pot hampers" as
these fruit baskets are called, takes about one hour and a
half to make and will stand several years rough usage.

Photo shows:- Mr. Venfield, who is carrying on the work of
his father, making "Pot hampers".
FOX.  1st June, 1942.  274848.

LONDON :  LONDONERS ARE GRADUALLY LEARNING HOW TO SCRAPE

FIRST OF BRITAIN'S NEW POWER STATIONS READY FOR ROYAL
OPENING.

Kingston, Eng: The first of Britain's 25 new power
stations - the 5 1/4 million sterling project at Kingston-
on-Thames, Surrey - is ready for the official opening
by the King on October 27.
The remainder of the 25 stations are scheduled for
completion by 1952 and will ease Britain's power shortage.
Shortage of labour has, however, created a bottleneck in
the building of the new stations for production of
generating plant has, according to a Ministry of Supply
official, outstripped the building programme.
The machinery is being stored until the stations are ready.

cheered the five wildly. Pit de-
puties held a final count, ticking

XH)           KENT HOP STRINGING COMPETITION

Believed to be the only contest of its kind in the world
the annual hop stringing competition, organised by The
Weald of Kent Ploughing Match Association, took place
to-day at Spitzbrook, Collier Street, Kent.  About 40
Kentish farmworkers, all experts in hop stringing, and
many of them coming from families which have worked in
the hop gardens for generations, took part.  The
stringer's job is to prepare hop gardens for the next
crop by putting up a complicated pattern of strings
which the hops can climb.  He works with a pole 10 feet
long, guiding the string (drawn from a bag slung over
his shoulder) from hooks in the ground to others hanging
on wires overhead.      He is followed by a "bander in"
(usually female) who binds together the groups of
vertical strings comprising a "hill."  In the
competition, each stringer completes a "cant" of 200
hills.  Some 40 miles of string are used in the
process.  Competitors score points for speed, neatness
and economy in the use of string.  The object of the
competition is to stimulate interest in the craft and
to encourage ability in a highly skilled branch of
agricultural work.

Photo shows:-  Miss A. Hewitt banding in for Mr. B.
King during the competition.

15/4/53           Topical Press       (Y 79669)

BRITAIN'S BIGGEST LAND PLANE.

The BRISTOL TYPE 167 low wing cantilever monoplane,
sometimes unofficially referred to as the BRABAZON I,
is the biggest land plane yet to be built by the
British aircraft industry and is now taking shape in the
Bristol Aeroplane Company's factory at Filton, Bristol.
Estimated to cost £4,000,000 the 167 is being
built solely for flight development work and is expected
to fly in the early summer of 1947.
The aircraft with an all up weight of 285,000 lbs,
- approximately 126 tons - will have a maximum level
speed of more than 300 m.p.h. at 25,000 feet, a cruising
speed of 250 m.p.h., at 25,000 feet, and a still air

Arrested Trawler
---
SIGHTING a French trawler, Notre Dame de Lourdes, within the three-mile limit off Rye Bay, early yesterday, the British gun-boat Kingfisher went alongside. The trawler moved off and Kingfisher followed her for 20 minutes, calling on her to stop.
Then, as she took no notice, the gun-boat fired a round of blank over her bows. The trawler came to a standstill, and later in the day her master was fined £10, including costs, at Dover, for being within British fishery limits.
The master, John Baptiste Margolle, blamed the flood tide for his being within the limit. All his gear was aboard.
There was no suggestion, said the Kingfisher's commander, that the trawl was down.
Top picture shows a customs official on the deck of the trawler in Dover Harbour; below, the officer is seen boarding the vessel from a customs launch. The gun-boat Kingfisher is in the background.

DESPITE claims by the tobaccon-
ists, who admittedly were thinking
of something rather different when
they elected actor Andrew Cruick-
shank as Pipeman of the Year last
month, Mr. Kenneth Foster must
be considered a strong contender
for the title.
Mr. Foster is a pipe inspector. As
may be deduced, he inspects pipes. But
the pipes he expertly studies are very
special pipes indeed—35 miles of them,
all intended to carry gas, or oil, from
the North Sea to Britain.
They have to be inspected because
at the moment, all these pipes are
steadily rusting away in a depot at
Great Yarmouth, Norfolk. It is a
process which is likely to continue for
some time—for the time, in fact, it
takes barristers, businessmen, preserv-
ationists and all to argue whether they
should be used to convey gas, or oil, to
a processing plant at Bacton, Norfolk.
A public inquiry begins today and
its machinations will take some time.
Depot officials are fatalistic: 'It
doesn't matter how long they rust
away. We can always brush them up.
And we know they'll be used some-
where.'
In the meantime, Mr. Foster carries
on inspecting. It won't be his fault if
the first North Sea gas (or oil)

title: A photographic print of Queen Elizabeth II and Prince Philip, Visit to Shetlands, August, 1960
description: A photographic print from the Daily Herald Archive folder: Queen Elizabeth II and Prince Philip Â» Visit to Shetlands Â» August, 1960.
gem_transcription_flat:
1983-5236/70139
---
ART LIBRARY
TO
PLEASE RETURN
11 AUG 1960
DAILY HERALD
PROPERTY OF
---
Shetlanders forgive the Queen
THE roar that greeted the Queen as
she stepped ashore in the Shetland
Islands yesterday told her: "All is for-
given."
Remember the bitter disappointment in
the Shetlands last summer when the
Queen's first-ever visit was cancelled on the
eve of her arrival? The baby was expected.
But the Shetlanders, whose hardy
womenfolk return to the fields 48 hours
after having their babies, are not people to
harbour a grievance.
"Thank you for such a forgiving wel-
come," said the Queen. She, too, remem-
bered the local criticism of her advisers
who were considered "too off-handed."
This was the first visit of a monarch to
the Shetlands since the Viking kings landed
700 years ago.
After the reception in Lerwick, the Queen
in flowerpot hat and loose coat of cyclamen
pink, faced a gale to meet the crofters and
fishermen in their lonely homes strung out
across Shetland.
Joking with the Lerwick lifeboat crew,
Prince Philip was told of their various
"landlubber" trades. He jibed: "I would
not like to go to sea with you lot."
But later he noticed a scroll for valour
on the wall. Every man of that crew had
an award for rescuing a Russian crew in
a midnight gale.
"I take it all back," said Philip.
---
DAILY
11 AUG 1960
HERALD
---
P2 8x4 3/8" deep

DAILY HERALD March 20 1959 5
Stolen—
a house
and all
mod. con.
Herald Reporter
FOUR cheerful young men took a pre-fab bungalow to pieces, loaded it in to a lorry, and drove away.
And that led to the strangest entry that police at Croydon, Surrey, have ever put in their log-book. It reads:
"Stolen; one prefab, with two bedrooms, lounge, kitchen and bathroom, fitted cupboards and all mod. con."
The prefab is — or WAS — in Firtree - avenue, Shrublands, Croydon. It was empty, and had been sold by Croydon council to a man in Suffolk, who was expected to take it away.
But the four young men beat him to it.
'A ROW'
As they worked, unhurriedly, neighbours watched, thinking they were contractors' men.
Mr. Charles Jones, a plasterer, who lives in the next house, said yesterday: "I was an innocent witness to the crime. I had a row with one of the men for flinging bits and pieces into my garden."
Police admit they haven't a clue — not even a finger-print.

gem_transcription_flat:
ARTHUR STEEL            22.2.66
LIFT TROUBLE IN COUNCIL FLATS
When the lifts in the huge blocks of flats are out of order(and this
oftens happen) old people and mothers with babies are trapped in their
flats as the stairs are unmanageable.
OPS...Mrs Carol Hammond and her children Gary 7, Ian 2 and Neal
10 months are often sealed off in their 9th floor flat in James
Hammett House, Bethnal Green.E.
---
TWICE a week, and sometimes
more, the world becomes a for-
bidden place for Carol Hammond
and her children. Inaccessible. Un-
attainable. Out of bounds.
Man may send Lunikular things
up to the moon, but the family
cannot even get down to ground
level. And if they could, they
wouldn't get up again.
So they stay put, trapped in their
ninth-floor home—the victims of lifts
which work if you're lucky but don't if
you're not.
The Hammonds are just one of the
families who suffer from liftlessness in
the Dorset Estate flats at Tower
Hamlets, London.
ONE-HOUR CLIMB
There's the woman of 76 who lives on
the 10th floor and needs support when
she walks.
When the lifts give up—"and some-
times they don't get fixed for days"—
her 74-year-old brother climbs up and
down the stairs to go shopping for her.
There's 58-year-old Albert Yeomans
who has asthma and lives on the
eighth floor. Once he took an hour to
climb the stairs.
So now, when he gets home and finds
the lift motionless he goes to his son's
home and sleeps there. Anything but
face those stairs.
Then there's Mrs. Ham-
mond, 28-year-old mother of
three young sons—Garry,
aged seven, Ian, who is two,
and 10-month-old Neal.
She says: "Whenever I want
to take the children out in the
pram I send Garry to make sure
the lift is working.
"If it isn't, I just give up
and stay home. This has hap-
pened too often to count."
The borough council are "dis-
tressed" about the situation.
New lifts have been ordered but
they are not expected for an-
other five months.
The borough's housing officer,
Miss Joan Simpson, said yester-
day: "The lifts do have a
harder life than those in blocks
of offices and luxury flats, be-
cause children tend to play
around with them.
"Tradesmen probably give
them a hard time, too, by jam-
ming the doors open while they
make deliveries. And perhaps
the lifts are simply getting old."
---
ARTHUR STEEL

She has a cure for
cigarette shortage
A SCHOOLGIRL has hit
upon an idea to end
the cigarette shortage.
She is Maureen Guerin, of
Silverdale - street, Kemp-
ston, Beds, and she writes to
the Daily Herald:
"I am just going to give you
a schoolgirl's idea of how the
problem of the cigarette short-
age might be solved.
"I have found out for myself
that many of the heaviest
cigarette smokers are women.
Why is this? In many cases it
is because women either dare
not or cannot smoke a pipe.
"Take, for instance, a woman
who dares not smoke a pipe in
public because she feels em-
barrassed. That woman can
only go on smoking her 20 or
30 cigarettes a day.
"Now if ladies' pipes were
designed to look attractive and
dainty, then I believe women
would go as crazy about them
as they did about slacks, which
really came from the men's
trousers."
When told of the idea, a
famous London firm of pipe-
makers said that they already
have a number of pipes at all
prices specially designed for
women (the one you see below
has a ring of diamonds set in
platinum round the stem, and
costs £9 10s.). Three or four
a week are sold.
Manager of another firm said
that he didn't think women
would go to the bother of fill-
ing and cleaning a pipe.
What do women smokers
think?

APRIL 9th. 1968.

HOP STRINGING COMPETITION.

          Hop stringers, the name given to men and women
who every year weave the vast "spider's web" of cord
yarn - some 300,000 miles of it - on which will grow
the hops required to flavour the nine thousand million-
odd pints of beer Britons can be expected to drink next
year, had their own competition in Kent today - the
Weald of Kent Ploughing Match Association's annual hop-
stringing competition - held at Pattenden Farm, Marden,
Kent.     The stringers carry the yarn in baskets slung
over their shoulders, and by means of poles, ten feet or
more long and tipped with iron tubing through which the
cord runs, thread it from pegs in the ground to hooks set
on wires 15 1/2 feet above the gardens.    The result is that
from each site of a growing hop plant, called "a hill",
arises a pattern of string resembling the spokes of an
umbrella - the name given to the type of stringing most
frequently met with in the South East.   The stringers,
who in the competition have to "string a cant of about
200 hills", are followed by assistants - usually women -
who act as "banders-in" and tie each group of four vertical
strings together about five feet from the ground.
---

By BARBARA MATTHEWS
IT WAS a magnificent bloomer, with a beautifully symmetrical crust and a crum that surpassed them all for its sheen, its even holes, its bluish tint and its superb aromatic flavour.
And it won the British Baker silver challenge shield, the bakery trade's most important trophy, at the Caxton Hall in London yesterday.
Mr. Sidney Geary, of Valley Bakeries, Ratby, Leics, carried off the shield on behalf of his son and partner, Charles, who actually baked the loaf.
Competition was fierce amongst different shaped loaves - bloomers, tins, farmhouses - and, in other categories of the contest, between hand-raised pork pies, Easter cakes with flop-eared bunnies, and scenes from Swan Lake, painted in confectioners' colours.
A loaf may seem a simple object beside these, but its judging was a complex ritual of prodding, stroking and sniffing (or, as bakers put it, testing the aromatic flavour).
Judges were looking for the sheen, the bluish tint a correctly-fermented loaf should possess, and the holes that prove there was still life in the dough.
"That is the way to make a loaf properly white," Mr. Geary told me. "Not bleaching the flour."
Mr. Geary's firm, three generations of bakers who supply about 150 Leicester shops, is what the trade considers a "small" baker. "We make our bread the old-fashioned way, although with modern equipment," he said.
"This loaf was baked on the oven bottom, and we managed to bring the dough to the peak of fermentation. It was a test of skill."

MANUFACTURING THE "FULLY FASHIONED".
NYLON HOSE IN THE MAKING.

British womenfolk are eagerly awaiting the
arrival in the shops of the supplies of Nylon hose -
items to bring a little luxury to the austerity ridden
legs of Britain. Stocking manufacturers throughout the
country are experimenting, calculating costs and planning
to produce sufficient quantities of stockings made of this
all wonderful, but mysterious material known as 'Nylon'.
Eventually Nylon stockings will be remarkably cheaply
produced, but initially it is expected that they will cost
about 15/- a pair, for 'fully fashioned' and about 8/11
for the 'semi' variety.

KEYSTONE PHOTO SHOWS: Miss Emily Claxton, is a "looper".
This entails sewing up the soles of the stocking without
leaving a seam. The job needs nine months experience
for real efficiency. Photograph taken at a British
Stocking factory.

B EMBRASURES FOR SANDBAGGED BUILT BLOCKHOUSES.
The weak feature in all rapidly constructed blockhouses
is the wooden framing used to form the opening.  The
opening does not protect the rifleman because the rim
can be penetrated by a bullet, also the splintered wood
carried away by the bullet can produce nasty wounds.
The present suggestion is to pre-cast the embrasure
opening of the desired aperture and angle, the outer
extremity having a light sheet steel framing embedded
in the face to prevent the concrete edges shattered by
a bullet from being detached and forming missiles.
The embrasure weighs less than 1½ cwt. and can easily

CROWN COPYRIGHT RESERVED. MINISTRY OF HOUSING & LOCAL GOVERNMENT.
Four prototype houses built for the Sheffield City Council by the
Public Works Department under the 5M system of construction devised
by the Research and Development Group of the Ministry of Housing
and Local Government. This system, which marks a new attempt to
bring the advantages of industrialisation into the field of house-
building, has been derived from the 5M CLASP system used at
Stevenage for a group of old people's flatlets. The new system
is called 5M, because as at Stevenage, it is based upon a planning
grid of 1' 8" (5 x the module of 4"). The object has been to
modify the CLASP system, which has been shown to have advantages in
the reduction of site labour and building time, to suit the
performance standards, and the levels of cost, of 2-storey housing.

---
USED
SUN
13 MAY 1969
---
Seconds after the launch the huge bulk of the Esso Northumbria makes the Tyne at Wallsend look like a ditch.
Not bad for a starter
PRINCESS ANNE launched her first ship yesterday with all the aplomb of a veteran.
She pulled a lever, sent a bottle of champagne crashing against the Esso Northumbria's bows, and the monster tanker slid smoothly into the river Tyne.
It was a faultless launch. The quarter-million-ton tanker, the biggest ever built in Britain, did not touch the opposite bank.
The ship made the Tyne at Wallsend look like a ditch. The tanker is 280ft. longer than the QE2, big enough to hide Buckingham Palace behind.
After the bottle-smashing, 40 seconds ticked away before the huge ship, towering above the Princess like a 10-storey building, started to move down the slipway.
As the ship gathered momentum and ploughed into the water, raising clouds of steam and dust, 10,000 people roared their approval.
The £6 1/2 million ship is the first of four ordered by Esso in Britain and was launched on time.
Afterwards Princess Anne, who was presented with a diamond brooch by the shipowners, said: "I have had the honour of launching the largest ship ever built in this country—and for a starter, that is not bad.
"I have experienced the warmth of a Tyneside welcome which has been overwhelming—two things I shall never forget."
Sir John Hunter, chairman of Swan Hunter, yesterday confirmed that the shipyard have won an order for another quarter-million-ton tanker from Anglomar Shipping of London, as reported in yesterday's Sun.
By FRANK DAWES
Shipping Correspondent

From their hiding places, the

the 5,600-ton oil-drilling rig, Sea

collapsed in the icy North Sea.

of ships searched the wreckage-strewn sea for
survivors from the ill-fated rig 40 miles off

---
THEY'RE BAKING BOATS FOR MASS PRODUCTION
February 15th 1958 PAR 69070-2 (Wo-R)

THEY'RE BAKING BOATS FOR MASS PRODUCTION

As sailing fast gains popularity as a sport,
modern mass production methods derived from
those developed during the war for making
wooden aircraft are being applied to the
manufacture of boats at the Hamble, Hampshire,
factory of Fairey Marine Ltd., a subsidiary of
the Fairey Aviation Company.
The craft are 'hot-moulded' from planks of
wooden veneer, a method which eliminates the
old and laborious method of boat-building by
individual craftsmen.
The shell of each boat is composed of layers
of planks applied to a mould to form 'skins'
glued together. Each shell is baked by
steam heat up to 100 degrees Centigrade for
about half an hour. Then it is taken out of
the oven and removed from the mould.
The resulting boat, it is said, will last a
lifetime and is proof against all the normal
ills which affect boats built by other methods.
More than 1,000 boats were produced at Hamble
in 1957, ranging from 7ft. 6in. dinghies to the
26ft. Atalanta sailing cruiser.
Over one-third of the output is exported.
PICTURE SHOWS:- The shell of a 15ft. Albacore
craft being placed in the oven for baking
at Hamble.

50 to 100,000 FULLY BOUND BOOKS PER WEEK.
Some of the largest Perfector printing
machines in Europe: Printing 64 pages on

The copy from the author goes to Linotype

Plates are assembled in special order on the

application of ink, the printed sheet is
produced.
The printed sheet goes through nearly half-
a dozen operations such as folding, gathering,

Real leather is used for the making of cases.

BRITAIN’S richest strike
of natural gas on land
has been made 6,000ft.
below a Yorkshire forest. A
24-hour test produced 10mil-
lion cubic feet of gas —
enough to supply a large
town.
 “It is a mighty big find,” said
French-Canadian Floyd Des-
rosiers, leader of a team who have
been drilling day and night for
four months.
 He added jubilantly: “We will do
even better when we drill down
another 1,500ft.”
 The drill at Lockton,
near Scarborough, is the
sixth sunk in the area by
Home Oil of Canada, at a
cost of about £100,000.
 Managing director Wil-
liam Ogilvie said: “We
hope we have struck lucky
this time.”
 CAUTION
 And the Gas Council added
to the gusher excitement
yesterday when they an-
nounced that their North Sea
rig Mr. Louie, can produce
12million cubic feet a day.
 Last night there were opti-
mistic hopes that Britain
and the North Sea may be
floating on one gigantic gas
field.
 The full potential of the
Yorkshire well may be
known in about a month.
 Mr. Desrosiers warned:
“Until we sink one or two
more drill holes we shall
have to temper our joy and
enthusiasm with some degree
of caution.”
 But he added confidently:
“There has never been any-
thing like this on land in
Britain. It is its biggest kick
in 25 years’ prospecting.”

alloy was inaugurated yesterday at the Redditch (near
Birmingham) works of High Duty Alloys, Ltd., by the

with the hydraulic system for operating the movable

Captain Robert Balls carried out
his one-man rescue operation after
the rig's 136ft.-high drilling derrick,
radio room and two cranes had toppled
into the raging sea, and three of its
18 legs had collapsed.
The crew were marshalled at the
undamaged end of the 300ft. by 200ft.
rig to await Captain Balls's helicopter.
As the gale raged on, the Ocean
Prince, moored 110 miles east of Scar-
borough, bumped and bored furiously
against the sea bed. And
last night crewmen esti-
mated that a third of the
rig had fallen into the sea.
Some of the rescued men
were taken to the rig Con-
stellation, 20 miles away,
and some were flown to
land.
Last night a spokesman for
the owners, Burmah Oil Explo-
ration, said the men on Constel-
lation would stay the night
there because of the storm.
Captain Balls, 32-year-old
father of three, was called from
his bed in a Scarborough hotel
at 6am. after a Mayday signal
from the rig.
TRICKY
At 6.45 am. he took off from
a Scarborough helicopter pad.
He flew out to the rig and landed
in howling winds.
He picked up 19 men and
transferred them to the Con-
stellation after a tricky landing.

Prince to pick up 18 men, whom
he took back to Constellation.
Back he went to Ocean Prince
to pick up the remaining 8 men
and take them ashore.
He deliberately did not refuel
until the final stage of the
rescue because he was overload-
ing the helicopter and balancing
the extra weight by running low
on fuel.

Fenby, near Grimsby, said later:

NEW FERGUSON TRACTOR - the FERGUSON 35 de-luxe (Diesel Model)

The Ferguson 35 de-luxe incorporates numerous entirely new features
resulting from 13 years of intense research. The famous Ferguson hydraulic
system has been revolutionised. In addition to raising and lowering an
implement and automatically keeping a plough or cultivator at a selected
depth on uneven ground, the new hydraulic system gives the tractor driver
perfect control of front, mid or rear-mounted implements.

A new dual clutch gives a "live", engine-driven power-take-off for
power driven implements such as mowers or balers. A six speed gear box pro-
vides a wide selection of gears for every job on the farm enabling full use
to be made of the 37 brake h.p.. An alternative, ground speed p.t.o. in
hay making or fertilising, irrespective of the gear selected.

Among the many other important new features are included more
precise and easier steering, two steering brake pedals on the right hand
side of the transmission housing, a new safety starter, safety fuel tank,
instrument panel with a combined tachometer, speedometer and hour meter,
foamed cushion seat and padded back rest. Also new is the styling in two-tone
Ferguson grey and metallic bronze.

=o-o-o-o-o-o-o-o-o=
---

BIRTH OF
A PREFAB.
CONVOY
They are putting up alu-
minium bungalow No. 6886
at Ockenden, Essex, where it
will provide a home for
someone on a waiting list.
From the other side of
England, a "Herald" re-
porter tells how he saw No.
6886 come off the assembly
line to swell the Homes Con-
voy.
MOTORING to the Bristol
Aeroplane Company's fac-
tory at Oldmixon, near Wes-
ton-super-Mare, I passed 15
"Homes Convoy" lorries in as
many minutes—carrying sec-
tions of aluminium bungalows
to all parts of the South.
9½ in a minute
It is just over two years since
Airoh bungalow No. 1 left this
factory, which produced Beau-
fighters during the war. Today
these cream and green prefabs are
leaving Oldmixon at the rate of 30
a day from the conveyor belt
where No. 6886 was born.
"Life" for No. 6886 started on
Thursday at 8 a.m. when its floors,
in four sections,
were con-
structed in Old
Nixon's No. 7
workshop. Later
in the day the
floors were
moved by over-
head crane to
the conveyor
belt for assem-
bly of kitchen
and bathroom units.
Moved by tractor to No. 8 work-
shop, No. 6886 acquired its walls,
windows, doors, and roof as its
four parts moved 9½ inches a
minute down the assembly lines.
On Friday, at 7.45 a.m., No. 6886
was about to enter the factory's
huge paint-spraying tunnel, where
the paint is treated with hot and
cold air.
At 10.15 it was driven out of the
factory
And at 3 p.m. it left the factory
gates—less than 20 hours after its
first part was assembled.
I talked to the four drivers
taking No. 6886 to Ockenden—an
11½ hours run. Ex-RAF "Erk"
Roy Shingfield said: "When
I drive along with a part of one
of these houses I think: 'Some
lucky one has got a home to live
in.'"
Roy is hoping to get married
next year, if he can get a house.

AIMED AT THE EXPORT TARGET: 
BOWS OF STEEL ARROWS OF ALUMINIUM    DG/HT

     If Robin Hood and his Merry Men  could return
to their legendary haunts under the Greenwood Tree,
they would be surprised to find that  their stout
yew bows  had been superseded by superior weapons
of the finest steel.  Arrows too, are no longer the
grey goose feathered shafts   which routed the French
at Agincourt.    The bowman of 1950 uses aluminium.
     With the export market  as their target, a well
known steel tubing firm in Birmingham (Messrs. Accles
and Pollock) are now making  the new  bows and arrows
in steel and aluminium.  The steel  long bows are
said by expert archers, to give   far better performance
and greater accuracy than wooden weapons. Orders for
them  have  been coming in from all parts of the world.
     Making the bows, involves 200 processes, almost
everyone byhand. Fourteen heat treatments   are needed
and the  thickness of the tapered steel tube from which
the bow is drawn has to be controlled within one-thousandth
of an inch.

PHOTO SHOWS:- "Bow-belle". This young lady is putting

RURAL CRAFTSMEN   IN THE FOREST OF DEAN

that Miss Littler, a volunteer in the employment
of the Flintshire War Agricultural Executive
Committee possesses the gift of water divining.
Miss Littler joined the Women's Land Army March 1941
and is one of 9 girls employed on gang work.
Recently they were working on a piece of land which
was constantly being flooded by a hidden spring.
Mr.J.T.Richards, the Executive Officer of the
Flintshire War Agricultural Executive Committee, had
made extensive efforts to have the spring located.
Finally, he asked the 9 members of the Women's Land
Army, who were clearing the land, to try with a
hazel stick to see if they could divine this spring.
Miss Littler was found to be the only one who
possesses this unusual gift.
Since Flintshire farmers have heard of this there
have been many requests for her services, to help
in reclaiming flooded land and so save hundreds
of pounds in drainage. Also farmers wish to use
her to help to discover water for sinking wells.
O.P.S.1.  The first step to becoming a Diviner
is to cut a forked twig from a hazel tree.
Miss Littler who is 19 years of age is seen on
right.

HERALD REPORTER
THE girl from behind the Post Office counter, the little lady who types those polite demands "Dear Sir, unless ..." and 3,000 other women from Government offices packed Central Hall, Westminster last night.

gem_transcription_flat:
1983-5236/61948
---
THE Consecration
of the new
Cathedral Church
of St. Michael here
today was a cere-
money of simple,
yet luxurious
beauty.
The simplicity was in
the small, central acts
of consecration; the
luxury was in the
splendour of the set-
ting, the richness of
the ritual.
AWE
There were first the
processions, 11 of them in
all, containing a Queen, a
Princess, nine arch-
bishops, a stiffening of
knights, innumerable am-
bassadors.
Last but one came the
Queen's procession, pre-
ceded by her Gentlemen-
at-Arms, those clinking,
grey old gentlemen who
supply these occasions
with a sort of instant awe.
YELLOW
The Queen, in yellow,
was received at the gate
of the old cathedral by
the Bishop of Coventry,
Dr. Cuthbert Bardsley,
and escorted to the west
door of the new.
In her procession
walked Sir Basil Spence,
the Cathedral architect.
Fanfares, drums, and
then, as they died down,
the business of consecra-
tion. A technical cere-
mony, which begins,
superbly, with the Bishop
shouting "Open the
door."
The small unconcealing
glass doors swing open
and the Bishop, hitherto
seen but unheard, is es-
corted in.
---
The Queen signs the Sentence of Consecration. Her name as first wit-
ness is followed by that of the Archbishop of Canterbury, Dr. Ramsey.
---
Coventry

26 OCT 1949
---
HIGHLAND POWER SCHEME NEARLY READY
Cpr. 25.10.49.
The North of Scotland Hydro-Electric Board's Tummel-Garry
scheme, is expected to go into operation at the end of this
year when parts of the Clunie dam are completed. The 386 foot
long and 65 foot high Clunie dam at the Eastern end of Loch
Tummel will raise the level of the Loch by 17 feet and
more than double its length. The water will flow through a
23 foot diameter tunnel for two miles to the Clunie Power
Station, where three turbo-alternators with a total capacity
of 57,000kws, will be in operation. To equalise the fluctuating
discharge from Clunie Power Station will be the primary
function of the 480 foot long 74 foot high dam at Pitlochry.
Here, the power station is incorporated in the dam, and two turbo-
alternators will have a generating capacity of 15,000 kws.
Both dams have a fish ladder to enable salmon to reach the
upper reaches of the River Tummel. The whole scheme will have
an annual output of about 300 million units, and will have
another dam on the upper reaches of the River Errochty which
will have a high water level nearly 1,100 feet above sea-
level. The picture shows:-
---
No.1. The upstream face of Clunie dam, now nearly completed.
The concrete structure has been painted black to forestall any
action of the peaty water, and to seal any minute cracks in the
face of the wall. Note the tiny figure of a workman half-way
up the face [illegible] on the right hand side.

LN 269016      TEA        LONDON BUREAU
BUILD THEIR OWN HOMES IN SPARE TIME.

LONDON: Clerks, builders, printing workers and
lorry drivers are among the 25 members of the
Camberwell Enterprise Housing Club, who are
building their own homes on a site at Crystal
Palace (South London). The idea was born two
years ago, now every night, and at weekends
and holidays, the men work on the houses.
Neighbours lend a hand and much of the work
is done at night with the aid of floodlights.
Special features of the homes will be a modified
form of central heating; a garage to each house;
and a new "Accotile" plastic tile flooring
throughout. Skilled, unpaid foreman is Bill
Clark, who with Len King, a building representative
during the day, works in the "site" hut with the
plans. Bill will be the first to move into one
of the new homes - in May. The project is expected
to be completed in two years time.

in the daytime - tests the door jambs of one of
the houses. REG BRUCE, a paint worker, and HARRY OTT

HOW would you like to move into a new luxury £4,600 home without a lawn of your own, a front gate or a fence to gossip over?
Open-plan houses like this are already a common feature of suburban life in America, Canada and Australia; on a smaller scale, they are also found on council estates in Britain.
But now, because of the high cost of land on private developments, "togetherness" living is spreading among the young families who are buying a brand new home of their own.
Castles
If you live on one of these estates, you share the expenses of a gardener to mow the communal lawn, the upkeep of service roads, shared drive-ins and planned gardens.
Traditionally, we British like our "castles." We fence ourselves in and keep the neighbours out with a privet hedge and a stout front gate.
But the old attitude is already changing in the face of the high cost of seclusion on the new building developments. Damer Gardens in Henley-on-Thames, Oxfordshire, is typical of these new developments.
Back gardens are divided by post and rail fences, though some residents are already reinforcing these with barriers of wattle.

description: A photographic print from the Daily Herald Archive folder: Industry Â» Fuel + Power Â» Oil + Petrol - British Oil Wells.
gem_transcription_flat:
DcH White 13/7/49
Oil search at Formby
8/ Sam Bromley watches mud circulating
from 216 ft below ground being brought
up to surface
---
THIS PRINT IS THE PROPERTY OF THE
"DAILY HERALD" ART LIBRARY
AND MUST BE RETURNED UNREPAIRED.
---
14 JUL 1949 REC'D
---
1983-5236/51467
---
SEARCH FOR OIL IN LANCASHIRE.
Somewhere beneath the sand-dunes of the Lancashire
coast, seven miles from Southport, lies a huge
untapped supply of oil.
Sixteen engineers who have just sunk a bore hole hope
to find it before their instruments register 7,500 ft.
They cannot go any deeper than that with their present
equipment and if they have not found it at that depth
they will try somewhere else.
An official at the D'Arcy Exploration Co, who is doing
the work, said "for ten years we have been getting 400
tons of oil a year from eight 'surface wells' at
Formby, but those wells are only 100 ft deep and we are
confident that a large oilfield, much deeper is
supplying them".
They tried three times before at Scarisbrick and
Bickerstaffe, but although they went down to 7,600 ft
they could not find the source.
Pointing to a thick, pinky fluid oozing out of a large
pipe alongside the towering derrick on the new site,
John Gibson the drilling superintendant explained
"that is the circulating mud which we pour down the
centre of the drill pipe, It seeps through the drilling
bit and brings up the small pieces of rock formation".
After the formation has been sieved out, the mud goes
back down the drill pipe.

Road work in connection with the London County Council's

A.A. Nugent, Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of

East India Dock Road, Brusnwick Road, Drew Street and

BROADCASTING THE SPRING SEED........
BATTLE FOR THE HARVEST BEGINS IN BRITAIN.

With the first few sunny days of Spring sunshine, farmers
all over Britain are ploughing and sowing with all speed to gain
the valuable time lost through floods and tempest throughout the
land..   More than six weeks have been lost through severe
Winter weather, and the farmers and their labourers toil from
dawn till dusk in the great battle for the harvest - sorely needed -
which is to follow their present efforts.
Down on Sir Peter Greenwell's estate at Caterham, Surrey, the
ground, still heavy with moisture, would not be ready for sowing
by mechanical means for several days to come - but time is precious
and the sowing is being done by hand to gain valuable hours........
PHOTO SHOWS:- Scattering the seed.   Labourers broadcasting barley
seed by hand at Tillingdown Farm, Caterham, Surrey.

title: A photographic print of Industry, Rubber
description: A photographic print from the Daily Herald Archive folder: Industry Â» Rubber.
gem_transcription_flat:
FIRST POST-WAR CARGOES OF RAW RUBBER ARRIVE IN ENGLAND.

The first raw rubber cargoes to reach this country from Malaya for
nearly four years are being discharged in London docks. At Tilbury
Dock a cargo of about 580 tons of rubber has been unloaded from
the "Benlawers" - a transhipment from Singapore, picked up at
Calcutta. It is the second shipment to be made by the Rubber Control
buying unit.  The first, a small shipment of 150 tons which was
brought by the "Almanzora" to Southampton, was held up by the
dockers' strike and finally reached London by rail. A third
consignment of 300 tons from Singapore was brought into Liverpool
by the "Clan Chisholm". A fourth - and much larger - rubber cargo
of 8,300 tons left Singapore on board the "Empire" on October 28th.
PHOTO SHOWS:- A cargo of raw rubber from Malaya being unloaded
from the "Benlawers" onto a barge at Tilbury Docks, Essex: the
bales of rubber, which weigh about 280 lbs. apiece, are swung
overboard in nets, and manoeuvred into place on the barge.
DAV 21 November 1945 PN

BY BASIL MORGAN
THE Queen pressed a small brass button yesterday—and set moving the giant rollers of Britain's most modern steelworks.
Then she watched the first 10-ton ingot start a spectacular half-mile journey to end up as a steel strip 100 yards long.
She was opening Richard Thomas and Baldwin's new £150million steelworks at Llanwern, near Newport, Monmouthshire.
It was a ceremony that nearly did not take place.
On Thursday night, an electrical fault put the whole chain of hot steel rollers out of action.
PUT RIGHT
An emergency squad of repair men worked through the night and on into the morning. They put the fault right only hours before the Queen arrived.
Later the Queen, who was accompanied by Prince Philip, saw the steelworks' computor room, where all processes are automatically tracked.
She took over one set of controls and altered the thickness of sheet steel being made for Jaguar cars.
From Hot Mills to High Jinks — that's the name of a five-year-old pony the Queen has bought for Princess Anne. An announcement last night said that the pony has already been delivered to the Royal Stables.

THE RETURN OF THE SWORD

Coronation Brings It Back to Popularity

The sword, ancient weapon of defence, has now
become a token of ceremony. It will be much in
evidence during the Coronation festivities.
Many sword cutlers have gone out of business
in this age of the atom, but one firm, The
Wilkinson Sword Company, of Acton, London, have
kept up the ancient industry. At present they
have orders for 2,000 swords. They are busy making
officers' ceremonial swords or refurbishing old ones
that will be used in the Coronation.
Some of the orders received have come from Overseas.
The firm has the market largely to itself
- even American manufacturers appear to have
gone out of business.
Ceremonial swords have not been a standard item
of officers' equipment in the Army since before the
war. Many orders have been placed by the Ministry
of Supply and service-owned swords are issued to
officers as required from a pool formed by
regiments. Nevertheless, many officers still possess
pre-war swords and hundreds of these have been
sent for renovation, which mostly involves
replating. The average cost of this work is about

destructiveness of man, and shortly they will both be

The engine of a Morris Mini-Minor
dismantled and laid out for inspection
at the BP Research Establishment at
Sunbury-on-Thames, Middlesex, to-day
(Thursday) at the end of a 100,000 miles
'static' motor oil proving trial for BP 'Visco-
static' motor oil.
MR. J. CLYDESALE, Foreman Mechanic,
is inspecting one of the parts. He was
responsible for all routine service
checks during the trial.
Six production cars, selected at random
from showrooms by the RAC, took part
in the test. They were a Ford Anglia,
Hillman Minx, 3.8 Jaguar, Morris Mini-
Minor, Triumph Herald 1200 and a
Vauxhall Velox. All successfully
completed the 100,000 miles, which
began on May 1st last year after all
the engines had been sealed.
Most of the driving was done on the
M 1 Motorway but the cars were also
taken on to town and country roads, and
hill climbs also featured in the trial.
The engines were stripped down under
RAC supervision at Sunbury-on-Thames.
March 8th 1962. PAR XX 94991-2 (Sa-G)

SHORTAGE OF COAL BRINGS BRITAIN'S BIG INDUSTRY
TO STANDSTILL
- - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -
4-2-47

The big Midlands car factory, the Rover Works, Birmingham
has been paralysed owing to the coal shortage. Cars for
export and home market were being made here. Day by day they
moved off the production line, till coal stocks dwindled
to nothing, as consumption, even with every economy, out-
distanced supply. Like many other factories, these works
are paralysed by the coal shortage, and the plant stood
silent for three days.

and no car has moved forward on
the assembly lines.

gem_transcription_flat:
1983-5236/42276
---
126-TON 'BRABAZON' NEARS COMPLETION, WILL FLY THIS SUMMER.

Under the hands of 700 workers, the world's biggest landplane
is nearing completion at the plant of the Bristol Aeroplane
Company at Filton, Bristol.
Designed to be the aerial counterpart of the 'Queen Elizabeth' -
world's greatest ocean liner - the plane is the 'Brabazon I',
the gigantic sections of which are almost ready for final assembly.
It is expected that the 126-ton monster will take the air
for the first time in May or June and that three other
Brabazons on order will be flying on the London-New York service
of British Overseas Airways by 1950.
The Brabazon is a high-altitude, long-range low-wing cantilever
monoplane which will accommodate 70 to 100 sleeping passengers
or 120 sitting passengers in the utmost comfort.  The
143-feet cabin will be pressurised to maintain an equivalent
cabin altitude of 8,000 feet while flying at 25,000 feet.
Crew will number 13, including five stewards.
Wingspan of the aircraft is 230 feet - almost twice that
of Britain's largest bomber, the Avro Lincoln - and the height
over the rudder is 50 feet.
Eight Bristol 'Centaurus' 18-cylinder, sleeve-valve,
air-cooled radial engines, each rated at 2,500 brake horsepower
for take-off, will give a maximum level speed of more than 300
miles an hour at 25,000 feet, and economical cruising speed
of 250 miles an hour at the same altitude, and a still-air range
of 5,000 miles.  Initial service ceiling will be 25,000 feet,
increasing as fuel is consumed.
PHOTO SHOWS:- Men working on the spacious interior of the
'Brabazon's' main passenger cabin.
AND March 31st 1947 PN.r.

WONDERFUL LABOUR SAVING DEVICE USED IN
CANADIAN HARVESTING.

EIGHT THOUSAND BUSHELS PER DAY CUT AND THRASHED
BY ONE MACHINE WITHOUT BINDING AND STOOKING.

What is believed to have been the greatest use made of
mechanical power in farming ever witnessed in Western
Canada was used in the recent harvesting at Aldersyde
Alberta. A combined reaping and threshing machine was
used which dispenses with the idea of cutting in the
first place and the usual stooking by hand labour for
sun drying. This machine is used when the wheat
is dry and is out, thrown in the thresher and the wheat
transferred into a huge tank. When this is full the
wagons are brought up into which the wheat is again
transferred and then on to the elevator. The
importance of the invention is that it dispenses with
cutting and stooking, also solves the problem the
Western Farmers have experienced in getting
harvesters at the important moment. The success
has been so great it is considered it will not
be long before these machines are used universally.

Photo shows:- General view of the combined harvester
and wagon emptying the grain receptable to get it
ready for its next operation.

description: A photographic print from the Daily Herald Archive folder: Home + Housing Â» Post War Â» Slums + Living Conditions (UK Wide).
gem_transcription_flat:
1983-5236/50523
---
PROBLEM OF A WOMAN AND SIX CHILDREN
---
Living in one room - a wooden fruit picker's
hut, on Wested Farm, Crockenhill, near Swanley,
Kent, is Mrs. May Cropp, her three children and a
further three grandchildren (offspring of one of her
daughters).
She is a squatter. There is no sanitation
anywhere near the hut - nor the usual amenities. The
hut leaks, is unsanitary, and is certainly not
weather-
proof.
How she came to be there does not matter - what
does matter is that she cannot get another home to
live - and owing to the bad state of affairs the
farmer, C.T.Miller, of Wested Farm, has asked the
police to evict them in the hope that they will
be found better accomodation.
As it is, the children - ranging from a few
months to six years - cannot possibly be properly
fed, clothed and educated - and there is no talk of
them going regularly to school.
In this cold weather, some of them are to
be seen playing in the mud around their "home".
The Dartford Rural District Council, under
whose jurisdiction their "home" comes, should look
into the matter - the farmer is certainly not to
blame - it is the best housing he can offer - even
to squatters.
PICTURE SHOWS:
2. Mrs. Cropp and children at the door of their
"home".
19836   4/12/46   John Topham, Sidcup, Kent.

CORMAR HI - TWIST

Carpets with a high twist pile are ever gaining in popularity as people
discover the advantages of a crush-resistant pile which shows no marks
of shading or scuffing. The twist in the fibre not only gives a beautiful
textured effect to a plain carpet: it also ensures that the pile is much
harder wearing.

Greenwood and Coope were the first to realise the advantages of man-made
fibres in twist pile carpets when they produced Hi-Twist, the hard twist
carpet made of 50% Courtelle/50% Evlan. This blend of Courtaulds fibres
is particularly suitable for a twist pile carpet: the thermoplastic
qualities of Courtelle mean that the twist in the pile can be set by heat,
just like the pleats in a skirt, and this twist is permanent.

Hi-Twist presents very few problems where soiling and cleaning are concerned.
The presence of Evlan in the carpet prevents any electrostatic charge
building up - it is this charge that attracts particles of dirt in acrylic
fibres. Even when normal domestic accidents occur and the carpet is stained,
it is no problem to clean because the Courtelle in the carpet means that it
shampoos beautifully and dries very quickly.

Kinky pile carpets not only look good - they also wear much better, and
so Hi-Twist, of course, qualifies for Courtaulds Extra Duty Label which
means that it can be used for any location in the home.

At 52/6d a square yard it is very good value for money.
---

Miss Alexa Smith,

October, 1964.

happy in her work. The "pit brow lassies" work an eight-hour

1983-5236/52981
---
KING AND QUEEN TO VISIT CORNISH CLAY INDUSTRY
WILL SEE ST. AUSTELL PIT

When the King and Queen visit the West Country at the end
of October, they will inspect the china clay factory at
St. Austell, Cornwall, where the industry of china clay
digging has been carried on for 130 years.
The valuable raw material is still being mined and exported
in increasing quantities for use in drugs, cosmetics,
paper, paint, rubber and pottery making.
The white hills which surround the Lower Ninestones Pit at
St. Austell, are often spoken of as the Cornish "Alps", as a
result of the sand which is transported from the pits, and
deposited at the tops.
PHOTO SHOWS:- This joined photograph shows a clear view
of the 200 foot deep Lower Ninestones Pit, from top
to bottom.

The hosing of clay down the side of the pit can be seen
on the left, while at the bottom, are the purifying pits
and the trolleys which take the remains to the top by
railway.
MD Oct 23rd 1947 PN g

THIS ROOMFUL of china is only part of the world's largest banqueting service. It was ordered by the government of Ghana and has just been completed by John Aynsley, a Stoke-on-Trent pottery firm.

 It's a good thing the service had not all been engraved; altogether there were over 18,000 pieces, from meat dishes to coffee cups. 
 The service was made in three stages. In 1960 4,800 pieces were turned out, in 1963 another 6,600 and now the last 7,000 have been completed. 
 Michael Gillow, the firm's managing director, says: "Removing the crest was a very tricky operation, but we have managed it." 
 Now the world's biggest banqueting service is strictly anonymous.

description: A photographic print from the Daily Herald Archive folder: Industry Â» Fuel + Power Â» Gas - Wells In Great Britain.
gem_transcription_flat:
ARTHUR STEEL SUN 3.1.66 
In a field at South Godstone a gas well and a team of testers. 
O.P.S. L. to R... Jean Cros (Beziers), Phillipe Neyron (Beziers), John 
Trewhella (Cornwall) Chief, Ken Atwood (Houston, Texas) engineer from Esso, 
and Jan Groenestein from Amsterdam.
---
FARMER John Collard tended his
cattle and sheep as usual yester-
day. He was philosophical about
the men ploughing through the
mud in his bottom field—even
though they have struck gas.
Said Mr. Collard: "It won't make
much difference to me even if large
quantities of the gas are found."
He's right, too. For in Britain all
mineral rights are vested in the Crown
(which means, in this case, the Ministry
of Power).
The prospectors, too, were philo-
sophical about their strike on the
Collards' 200-acre farm at South
Godstone, Surrey.
Cornishman John Trewhella, who now
lives at Alkmaar in Holland, said:
"Optimistic? That's too strong a word.
We're just hopeful."
Mr. Trewhella, who
heads the team of con-
tractors called in to assess
the quality and quantity
of the strike, said: "We
will be testing for a week
or 10 days. Then we
should know how much
gas is here."
STRIKE
The search for gas down
on the farm began long
before the North Sea hunt.
The Esso Petroleum Com-
pany were granted prospect-
ing licences six years ago.
They negotiated agreements
with landowners in Hampshire,
Sussex, Kent and Surrey—and
began drilling four years ago.
From Mr. Collard they rented
a field on Langham Park Farm
where villagers had played foot-
ball for nearly 40 years.
And it was there that Esso
scored with an international
team captained by 37-year-old
Ken Atwood, of Houston, Texas.
Working with him and Mr.
Trewhella are Dutch and
French drilling experts.
Their strike is just off the
main London-Eastbourne road
—23 miles from London—oppo-
site Gus Rossini's transport
café.
GUSHER
Mr. Rossini said last night:
"When the gas is gushing, it's
lit. And the flames reach 30ft.
high or more. Then it's like a
fairground round here."
Friends who don't know about
mineral rights optimistically tell
Farmer Collard: "You'll be a
millionaire..."
But with an appropriate agri-
cultural turn of phrase, Mr.
Collard commented: "They're
counting my chickens before
they are hatched."
Brightening, he added: "We
must get a private pipeline.
After all, we cook with gas."

Now nearing completion in readiness for the launching
ceremony on December 17th at Messrs John Brown's shipyard

THE ROYAL SHOW  1963.                PC/

The Royal Show 1963 is taking place at
Stoneleigh Abbey Park, near Kenilworth,
Warwickshire.  For nearly one hundred
and twenty five years the Royal Show has
been taking place annually in various
parts of the country - it has now returned
to the Midlands to Stoneleigh Abbey, the
seat of Lord Leigh, which is hoped will
become its permanent site.  During the
many years the show has been taking place,
a great deal of changes have been made
to its presentation - and this years new
feature is the helicopter service from
which visitors can get an overall view
of the enormous area covered by the show
rings and exhibition stands. During the
build-up for the show the extremely bad
and wet weather has caused much havoc
but thanks to the herculean efforts made
by all concerned the show will go on as
usual. H.M.Queen Elizabeth II and the
Duke of Edinburgh, (President of the Royal
Agricultural Society of England this year)
will visit the show on Thursday, 4th. They
are expected to enter the main ring in a
carriage drawn by Windsor Greys.

PHOTOGRAPH SHOWS:-   An aerial view of

gem_transcription_flat:
1983-5236/47959
---
THE MODERN GIRL PLIES A CENTURIES-OLD TRADE
July 13th 1953 PAR 36404 -2 (BKS-R)
_________________________________________________________
THE MODERN GIRL PLIES A CENTURIES-OLD TRADE

For at least seven centuries, the manufacture
of nets, ropes, sailcloth and other hempen
products has been the staple industry of
the town of Bridport, Dorset.
Of Bridport's present-day population of about
6,000, over a thousand - many of them young
women - are engaged in the industry,
directly or indirectly.
At one time locally-grown flax and hemp were
used, but nearly all the raw material is
now imported.
It is recorded that all the ropes and sails
for King John's Navy (he reigned from
1199-1216) were made at Bridport. And the
expression 'stabbed by a Bridport dagger' for
a person who had been hanged was current
in 1530, when King Henry VIII reigned.
This picture was taken in the Bridport works
of Joseph Gundry and Co. Ltd., a firm founded
in 1665 and still controlled by lineal
descendants of the founder. There were
Gundrys engaged in the trade as early as 1580.
PICTURE SHOWS:- PHYLLIS STROUD, attractive
representative of modern Bridport,
'squaring through' a length of netting
with a knife.
July 13th 1953 PAR 36404-2 (BKS-R)

FOR FIRST PUBLICATION IN EVENING
PAPERS OF TUESDAY, JULY 14th.
---
PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
RCD. 15 JUL 1953
PLEASE RETURN
TO
ART LIBRARY
